themes.theme: Whether to use AI at all
themes.definition: Tests a body is asked to apply before choosing AI for a problem: need, proportionality, comparison with alternatives, and the balance of benefit and risk.
themes.what_is_set_out: Most guidance documents ask the body to test AI against the problem before adopting it, rather than leaving adoption open. UK174 is the most emphatic: use cases 'must be led by business and user needs, pain points and inefficiencies, not what the technology can do', AI should be used 'only when relevant, appropriate and proportionate', and 'Where these risks are too high, you must reconsider if AI should be used at all'; UK099 asks teams to 'explore different options, including not using AI at all' and not to use a system that cannot be made 'sufficiently safe for the intended use'. UK268 and UK010 make the test comparative: AI 'should demonstrate clear, measurable benefits compared with conventional approaches' (UK268), and stakeholders articulate benefits and risks 'compared with alternative or traditional technologies' (UK010); UK266 turns the same test into audit-committee questions on business need, value for money, technical feasibility, an ethical outcome and realistic scale, and UK136 builds it into procurement ('be open to alternative solutions'; no procurement discussion 'if no data will be available'). Cost and energy enter as reasons not to use generative or agentic AI (UK174, AI_Insights), equality must be considered 'at the start' of the decision (UK216), and the ATRS template asks bodies to record the alternatives they considered but accepts 'N/A', so considering alternatives is not itself required there. None of these passages defines the threshold ('too high', 'sufficiently safe') or names who makes the call beyond 'you' or 'the organisation'.
themes.holders: 'You' (government departments, public sector organisations and their teams) in UK174, UK099 and AI_Insights; 'organisations' in UK266 and UK268; energy-sector 'stakeholders' in UK010; central government procurement teams in UK136; public bodies in England in UK216; bodies completing ATRS records (UK087). UK266 puts the questions in the mouths of audit and risk assurance committees.
themes.binding: Mostly 'should', 'consider' or questions in non-statutory guidance. UK174 and UK266 use 'must' without any stated enforcement. The equality timing in UK216 rests on the statutory equality duty as interpreted by the EHRC, with legal action named as a possible consequence of breach. No document states what happens if the test is skipped.
themes.checks: The test is itself an assessment made before adoption. Trigger: before use (early, at discovery, before procurement, before choosing a technical approach). Compared against: business and user need, conventional or alternative approaches, value for money, the body's own risk tolerance. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: not named beyond 'you' or the organisation; in UK266 audit and risk assurance committees ask the questions. What happens with the result: reconsider, choose an alternative, terminate or do not use; otherwise not stated.

themes.theme: Risk appetite, risk tiers and accepting residual risk
themes.definition: Who sets how much risk an AI use may carry, how risk tiers scale the scrutiny a tool receives, and who formally accepts risks or bias that remain after mitigation.
themes.what_is_set_out: Several documents make the body's own risk appetite the yardstick for AI decisions, rather than an external limit. UK174 asks organisations to 'make a strategic decision on how any use of AI technology fits with your existing risk tolerance'; UK010 says that for black-box AI 'the organisation must decide as to whether it can tolerate the risk'; the NAO plans to 'Refine risk appetite, thresholds and escalation routes based on experience'; AI_Insights asks senior leaders to 'Define a risk appetite' for records disposal; and UK082 says government 'will need to be prepared to absorb some risk'. Risk tiers then set how much scrutiny a tool gets: UK071 has an initial risk classification 'guide the depth of testing', the NAO gives higher-risk uses 'greater scrutiny and assurance' while lower-risk use can 'scale more rapidly', UK206 lets low-risk uses rely on fewer assurance techniques, UK268 ties audit depth to risk, and the AI_Insights bias guidance adds a human in the loop at High risk and 'Mandatory human approval decisions' at Critical risk. Accepting what remains after mitigation is named in UK071 (ethical or safety issues 'must be addressed or explicitly accepted by governance if not fixable'; remaining disparity 'consciously signed-off with rationale'), and trade-offs between principles or mitigations must be weighed in UK099 and AI_Insights. None of these passages defines tier boundaries or numeric tolerances; the NAO's tiers and the AI_Insights Critical level are not defined in the coded text.
themes.holders: The organisation or 'you' (UK174, UK010, UK206, AI_Insights); the NAO, whose Executive Team holds risk appetite; 'governance', not further named (UK071); senior leaders (AI_Insights); government (UK082); auditors deciding audit depth (UK268, nearest actor).
themes.binding: Guidance verbs ('should', 'critical', 'must' inside lists of considerations); NAO organisational commitments; UK082 recommendations in an independent report whose acceptance is not recorded in the text. No consequence is stated for acting outside the stated appetite.
themes.checks: Initial risk classification (UK071): trigger before testing; compared against factors such as impact on legal rights, safety, scale of use and novelty; threshold not stated; who not stated; result sets the depth of testing. Risk acceptance (UK071, UK010): trigger after testing and mitigation; compared against the body's risk appetite or tolerance; threshold not stated; who is 'governance' or 'the organisation'; result is fix, accept with a recorded rationale, or do not proceed [inference for the last]. Bias trade-offs (AI_Insights): thresholds defined by the organisation and mapped to regulatory requirements; values not stated.

themes.definition: Points at which a named body or person must approve an AI tool, use case, deployment or spend before it proceeds.
themes.what_is_set_out: Named approval points are clearest in departmental policy. DWP's policy (UK190) makes the Digital Design Authority 'the lead DWP governance board for the approval of new digital tools and the use cases of digital tools', makes the AI Delivery Board 'the formal sign-off board for AI implementation across DWP', limits use to approved tools, requires governance-board approval before sensitive data are used, and warns that a pilot approval may need further engagement before larger-scale use; how the two boards relate is not stated. UK174 recommends an AI governance board 'to set principles and review and authorise uses of AI', cybersecurity-team approval of supporting tools, Secure by Design compliance 'before it can be deployed', and restates mandatory assurance-board approval of spend above £100,000 (digital) or £1 million (technology). UK071 puts approval at go-live ('for high-risk AI, this may require senior approval or an ethics board decision'), with a stakeholder sign-off session as the final gate and go/no-go held by SROs and governance boards; UK268 treats project-proposal approval as common practice and makes release 'contingent on passing all pre-deployment evaluations', but names no approver beyond the product owner accepting deliverables. AI_Insights requires 'written approval and confirmation from a manager or responsible officer' before user-built agents are activated, and makes the KIM team decide when a model is 'relevant and accurate enough' to base retention decisions on; the NAO's AI Governance Board reviews higher-risk use cases (approval implied, not stated), UK010 says the AI strategy may need board agreement, and the ATRS team gates publication of a record, not use of the tool, on written confirmation of internal sign-off. Outside DWP, approval is mostly 'should' or 'may', and the approving body is often left to the organisation.
themes.holders: DWP's Digital Design Authority, AI Delivery Board and 'relevant governance board'; an organisation's AI governance board, cybersecurity team and assurance boards (UK174); 'senior approval or an ethics board', SROs and governance boards, and relevant stakeholders such as an ethics board, data privacy office and domain leaders (UK071); a manager or responsible officer, KIM professionals and the KIM team (AI_Insights); the NAO AI Governance Board; the board or equivalent governing body (UK010); the ATRS team (UK086). Not stated in UK268's release gate.
themes.binding: Mandatory by departmental policy in DWP ('must'), with line managers acting on non-compliance under DWP's discipline policy (as the coder records for policy statement 2). Spend approval is described as 'mandatory' and Secure by Design as a pre-deployment condition in UK174. Elsewhere 'should', 'may' or descriptive. The consequence of skipping a gate is otherwise not stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: before use of a tool or use case, before go-live, before spend, before activating an agent, before scaling a pilot. Compared against: the board's principles (UK174); acceptance criteria and pre-deployment evaluations (UK268, UK071); Secure by Design principles (UK174); the rules, guidelines and guardrails the organisation has set (AI_Insights, per coder note). Metric or threshold: spend thresholds (£100,000 and £1 million) are stated; otherwise not stated, and 'relevant and accurate enough' is undefined. Who: as listed under holders. What happens with the result: approval or refusal; what follows a refusal is not stated.

themes.definition: Requirements that tests, evaluations or impact assessments be produced and used as the basis for deciding whether a tool proceeds, scales, is adjusted or stops.
themes.what_is_set_out: Several documents tie checks to decisions, but differ in how firmly. UK268 states that test results and evidence of meeting acceptance criteria 'form the basis for the go/no-go deployment decision', for in-house and purchased systems alike, and that a system changed by a vendor update returns to production only 'once it passes all relevant tests'; UK071 states that 'no AI system is deployed without adequate testing', makes data validation yield an ‘OK to proceed’ signal or 'Decision note' before training, and has testers' recommendations 'feed into the governance decision-making'. UK133 (HM Treasury) is permissive: formative testing and 'rapid evaluations can be used' to decide whether an intervention moves to testing at scale and full roll-out, with no decider named. Impact assessments serve as decision points: UK216 (EHRC) asks 'can you continue or should you stop and remove the proposal or service?' and applies this to AI 'developed outside of your organisation'; UK099 treats an equality impact assessment with acceptable risks as the point to start building; UK136 asks impact assessments to include ‘go/no go’ key decision points. AI_Insights says an AI solution that 'fails this evaluation' goes back to development or redesign and warns against moving prototypes 'straight to production', and UK266 asks whether decisions 'to stop, scale or redesign' will be made 'based on evidence'.
themes.holders: Mostly not stated. 'Governance', not further named (UK071); the organisation (UK268), with the product owner accepting deliverables per its roles appendix; public bodies in England (UK216); 'you' or the project team (UK099, UK136, AI_Insights); the organisation deploying a system (UK206); audit and risk assurance committees asking (UK266).
themes.binding: Good practice or recommendation throughout; UK133 is descriptive ('can be used', 'may then be used'). UK216 rests on the statutory equality duty as the EHRC reads it. No consequence beyond not proceeding is stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: before training (data validation, UK071); before deployment (UK268, UK071, AI_Insights, UK206); before scaling or full roll-out (UK133, UK266); after a vendor update or model change (UK268); when developing a proposal or reviewing an existing service (UK216). Compared against: acceptance criteria agreed in advance (UK268); benchmarks and success criteria (UK071, AI_Insights); equality impact (UK216); the Theory of Change (UK133, coder note). Metric or threshold: not stated in these passages; 'adequate' testing is defined only by proportionality to risk (UK071). Who: testers and teams produce the evidence; the decider is usually not named. What happens with the result: go or no-go, return to development or redesign, adjust, continue, or stop and remove.

themes.theme: Setting acceptance criteria, metrics and thresholds
themes.definition: Requirements to fix in advance the performance, fairness or benefit criteria against which an AI tool and its outputs will be judged, and who sets them (a split of the starting code 'setting standards').
themes.what_is_set_out: The documents that address this leave the yardstick to the deploying body but ask that it be fixed in advance and justified. UK268 has the project or product owner 'decide on which performance measures are required from the AI system and the acceptance of the deliverables', asks that 'acceptance criteria are clear and agreed in advance', and expects organisations to define and justify performance metrics and fairness metrics that 'align with legal and policy requirements', considering individual and group fairness, plus benefit indicators from the outset and post-deployment benefit targets. UK071 gives the only numeric illustration (“model must achieve 90% accuracy on benchmark X” or “no disproportionate impact greater than Y between groups”), asks teams to define which protected attributes matter for fairness, and offers a set of quality attributes as the comparator. AI_Insights asks organisations to define 'acceptable bias thresholds' mapped to their risk tolerance and to regulatory requirements, to treat fairness as a priority 'alongside traditional metrics, such as accuracy and latency', and, for records tools, to 'Set your benchmarks before you begin the development process' so human reviewers can test against them, resetting benchmarks when a solution is reused; UK206 poses the question 'Is some bias acceptable?'. No passage sets a binding threshold, and none makes consistency or repeatability of outputs, prompt or configuration control, or fixing a model version an acceptance criterion.
themes.holders: The project owner or product owner (UK268 roles appendix); 'organisations' (UK268, AI_Insights); the team, not named (UK071); 'you' and the KIM team, with human reviewers doing the testing (AI_Insights); the organisation deploying the system (UK206).
themes.binding: Auditor expectations ('should expect') and expected controls in UK268; recommended practice in UK071; 'must' in non-binding guidance in AI_Insights; a question in UK206. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: criteria set before development or testing ('in advance', 'from the outset'), and reset on reuse (AI_Insights). Compared against: legal and policy requirements (fairness metrics, UK268); conventional approaches (benefits, UK268); risk tolerance and regulatory requirements (bias thresholds, AI_Insights). Metric or threshold: accuracy, disparity between groups, fairness metrics, latency, false positives and false negatives (the coder note to UK-DM-DES-230 gives under 1% false positives and about 5% false negatives as examples); all numbers are illustrative and the threshold is left to the body. Who: the product owner or organisation sets the criteria; human reviewers test against them (AI_Insights). What happens with the result: it feeds the acceptance and go/no-go decision (see 'Evidence feeding the go/no-go decision').

themes.theme: Automated deployment gates and automatic rollback
themes.definition: Arrangements under which a pre-set metric threshold, rather than a person, blocks a release or reverts a model, with people alerted afterwards.
themes.what_is_set_out: Only the AI_Insights article on bias in large language models sets this out, and it is the one place in this cell where stopping or reverting a tool is triggered by a pre-set threshold rather than decided by a person. The continuous integration pipeline 'should incorporate automated bias evaluation as a mandatory gate, and block deployments that exceed predefined thresholds regardless of improvements in other metrics', and deployment gates 'should enforce hard blocks on threshold breaches'. In production, for critical applications where bias incidents could cause harm 'before human responders can act' (coder note), the system 'automatically reverts to the last known fair model version while alerting engineers to investigate the problem'; the risk matrix lists 'Auto-rollback on threshold breach' at Critical risk. Content classifiers may run in 'blocking mode' or 'flagging mode', the choice depending on the application's risk tolerance and the classifier's accuracy (coder note). The thresholds are set by the organisation (see 'Setting acceptance criteria, metrics and thresholds'), so the automatic gate enforces a human-set yardstick [inference]; no other document in this cell provides for automatic stopping.
themes.holders: No human holder for the gate itself: the CI pipeline or deployment gate acts automatically. Engineers investigate after a rollback; organisations set the thresholds; a human reviewer takes the final decision in flagging mode.
themes.binding: 'Should' in non-binding GDS guidance; the risk matrix presents auto-rollback as a mitigation required at Critical risk. Stated effect of a breach: deployment blocked or model reverted.
themes.checks: Trigger: every deployment through the CI pipeline; continuous monitoring in production. Compared against: predefined acceptable bias thresholds, and the last known fair model version. Metric or threshold: bias metrics; threshold values not stated. Who: automated; engineers investigate root causes and develop permanent fixes. What happens with the result: the release is blocked regardless of gains in other metrics, or the model automatically reverts to the last known fair version and engineers are alerted; in flagging mode, suspect content goes to a human for a final decision.

themes.theme: Change control and re-approval after deployment
themes.definition: Requirements that updates, retraining, vendor model changes or significant changes of use go through a controlled and approved process and can be reversed (a split of the starting codes 'approved' and 'paused or stopped').
themes.what_is_set_out: Changes after go-live are treated as new decisions in several documents, with DWP the most specific. DWP (UK190) says that 'Where there is a significant change to the use case of an approved AI tool, for example using personal data where it was not used before, this change must be approved by a relevant governance board', and that a pilot approval may need further engagement before larger-scale use. UK071 says changes from retraining or new data 'must go through a controlled process with re-testing and governance sign-off'. UK268 asks that 'Change management processes must be in place to govern future updates, migrations, and rollbacks', that after a vendor update or model change that 'materially affects system behaviour' the system is re-tested against its acceptance criteria before returning to production, and that policies exist for retraining when drift is detected. UK174 sends model updates through a 'managed release process' (coder note) that can be withdrawn and reverted 'to an earlier version', and asks teams to set out 'who has the authority to change and modify the code of the AI model'; UK010 lists 'robust change control' as a governance consideration, and AI_Insights asks for new benchmarks when a solution is reused. 'Significant' and 'materially' are not defined beyond DWP's example.
themes.holders: A 'relevant governance board' (DWP); 'governance', not further named (UK071); the organisation (UK268); 'you' and teams (UK174); energy-sector stakeholders (UK010); the KIM team (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: Mandatory by departmental policy in DWP; 'must' in a framework that describes itself as non-mandatory (UK071); good practice ('must' and 'should') in UK268; 'should' and 'need to' in UK174; a consideration in UK010. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: on change — updates, retraining, migrations, vendor updates or model changes, a significant change of use case, detected drift, reuse of a solution, scaling beyond a pilot. Compared against: the original acceptance criteria or benchmarks (UK268, AI_Insights); re-testing (UK071). Metric or threshold: not stated; 'significant' and 'materially' undefined. Who: a governance board or 'governance' signs off; the organisation re-tests. What happens with the result: approval and return to production, or withdrawal and reversion to an earlier version.

themes.definition: Provisions for stopping an AI tool temporarily or permanently, reverting it, or keeping services running without it.
themes.what_is_set_out: The documents agree that it must be possible to stop or reverse an AI tool, but none of these passages names who decides to do it. UK174 requires mechanisms 'to investigate any areas highlighted by users, and make changes to or decommission AI systems if unacceptable risks or harms are identified', contingency and fallback processes so services continue if a system is stopped, and says 'you must consider terminating the project' if negative consequences are too high; UK099 says 'You must retire all platforms at an appropriate time', with triggers including the public benefit no longer being met (coder note). UK268 asks for corrective action '(such as retraining, technical adjustments, or decommissioning)' when performance or compliance requirements are no longer met or the business need changes, defined 'triggers for decommissioning', and rollback or decommissioning after security incidents. UK071 lists 'Safe shutdown and kill switches' in operational acceptance testing, an incident response plan that answers 'What triggers rollback?', the ability to 'roll back a model', and decommissioning criteria (obsolete, outperformed, risk exceeds benefit, per coder note). AI_Insights notes that end users 'could turn off the model' in their own accounts, and UK216 and UK266 frame stopping as a question to ask; thresholds such as 'unacceptable' and 'too high' are left undefined throughout.
themes.holders: 'You' or the organisation (UK174, UK099, UK268); the team, not further named (UK071); end users for their own accounts (AI_Insights); public bodies in England (UK216); organisations running pilots (UK266). The decision-maker for stopping is not stated in any passage.
themes.binding: 'Must' in non-statutory guidance (UK174, UK099); good practice (UK268); recommended core practice and critical considerations (UK071); questions (UK216, UK266). No consequence is stated for failing to stop a tool.
themes.checks: Trigger: user reports; unacceptable risk or harm identified; security incidents; failure to meet performance or compliance requirements; a changed business need; a tool obsolete or outperformed; risk exceeding benefit (all ongoing, after deployment). Compared against: performance and compliance requirements (UK268); benefit against risk (UK071, UK174). Metric or threshold: not stated (the coder note cites UK071's example metric 'Mean Time to Shutdown'). Who: not stated. What happens with the result: changes, retraining, rollback to an earlier version, temporary or permanent stop, or decommissioning with data archived or deleted; essential services kept running through fallback or contingency plans.

themes.definition: Rules about which decisions must stay with a human decision-maker, with AI limited to supporting them, and how tasks are divided between people and AI (a split of the starting code 'overriding outputs').
themes.what_is_set_out: The firmest rule in the cell is UK174's restatement of data protection law: 'Services using AI that affect a person’s legal status or their legal rights must only use AI to support decisions that must be made by a human decision maker', with the human input needing to be ‘meaningful’ (coder note); UK174 also says AI 'should not be used on its own in high-risk areas' and cautions against fully automated significant decisions. UK099 asks teams to avoid fully automated decisions where the outcome 'could significantly affect individuals or groups' and to make sure 'a person makes the final decision in these cases'. AI_Insights requires that 'no critical decisions are made by these entities without human expert insight', that responsibilities are not 'automated away', and that there is a human in the loop 'whenever your AI model is making decisions that your organisation would normally expect to account for'; in records review the AI recommends and people 'authorise disposal actions', and its bias risk matrix requires a human in the loop at High risk and human approval at Critical risk. The NAO commits to AI that augments 'rather than replace' professional judgement, UK268 asks that 'Human and AI roles should be clearly defined', and the ATRS template asks bodies to disclose 'What decisions or processes does the tool's output inform or support?'. The trigger words ('significant', 'critical', 'high-risk', 'qualified people') are not defined, and only the legal-status rule rests on statute.
themes.holders: Services using AI that affect legal status or rights, and 'you' (UK174, UK099); DSIT speaking as 'we', and organisations deploying AI models (AI_Insights); the NAO; organisations completing ATRS records (UK087). The human decision-maker is not further named ('a person', 'qualified people', 'human expert insight').
themes.binding: The legal-status rule has a statutory basis (UK GDPR; the coder records that breach 'may infringe the UK GDPR'), and UK174 notes that a legislative framework may itself require a decision to be made by a particular person. The rest is 'should', 'need to' or 'must' in non-binding guidance, or an organisational commitment (NAO).
themes.checks: Not a check in itself, but it sets which cases must reach a human. Trigger: decisions affecting legal status or rights; high-risk or significant decisions; critical decisions by agents; decisions the organisation would normally be expected to account for; High and Critical risk tiers. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: none; confidence scores or sampling rates are not used to route cases to a human. Who: a human decision-maker, not further named. What happens with the result: the human makes or approves the final decision and the AI output is advisory.

themes.theme: Human review and override of outputs
themes.definition: Arrangements by which people review, correct, approve or override what an AI tool produces before it takes effect, and the authority they hold when they disagree with it.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 requires that 'humans validate any high-risk decisions influenced by AI' and that there are 'strategies for meaningful intervention', and, for AI that triggers actions, that 'there must be a human present to review the action before carrying it out'. UK099 says 'People must be able to monitor and influence how systems work, even when the system is partially or fully automated', and recommends a human in the loop 'to oversee and validate outputs and decisions' in risky or high-impact uses, able to 'identify risks and intervene'. UK268 asks guidance to settle 'authority and accountability in case of disagreement' between AI systems and case workers; UK071 makes 'Human oversight and override capabilities' a critical part of operational acceptance testing (example metric: override rate, per coder note) and asks 'when does a human need to override or question the model?'. AI_Insights is the most concrete about particular uses: merges of AI-assisted code 'need to be subject to human peer review', developers 'should only commit code changes that you understand', HITL systems 'review, correct and approve system output', flagged content goes 'for human review for a final decision', and a department needs 'a clear process ... to check and approve your review decisions before they are actioned', with the organisation deciding who is in the loop, at what stage and at what scale. Which cases reach a human is set by risk category or criticality, not by confidence scores, sampling or error rates, which no passage specifies.
themes.holders: 'You' and teams (UK174, UK099); a human-in-the-loop person or team; operators (UK071); case workers (UK268, UK071); developers and one or more peer reviewers (AI_Insights); the department approving review decisions (AI_Insights); end users who can retrain or switch off a model (AI_Insights, experimental ideas).
themes.binding: 'Must' and 'need to' in non-statutory guidance (UK174, UK099); good practice (UK268); critical consideration or recommended practice (UK071); 'need', 'should', 'vital' and 'can' in AI_Insights. No consequence is stated for absent review.
themes.checks: Trigger: before an AI-triggered action is carried out (UK174); before code is merged (AI_Insights); before review decisions are actioned (AI_Insights); ongoing in risky, high-impact or critical uses (UK099, UK174, AI_Insights); override capability tested before deployment (UK071). Compared against: the reviewer's own judgement and the facts of the case (the UK071 caseworker example in the coder note), and the organisation's policies. Metric or threshold: override rate is given as an example metric (UK071); otherwise not stated. Who: human reviewers, peers, case workers, operators, the department. What happens with the result: the output is approved, corrected, overridden or rejected; what follows a failed review is not stated.
